title: When do we round up and when do we round down?
description: A school of seven hundred thirty two people needs sweets, and an item costing four hundred seventy rupees is called around four hundred fifty. The board shows which approximate number is more than the real one and which is less, and gives a situation for each kind of rounding. Keeko then raises a hand, thinking seven hundred sweets are enough.
teaching_notes: One idea: an approximate number is rounded up when it is more than the real number and down when it is less, and the situation decides which is safe. Ask the class what is wrong with too few sweets before any number is chosen. Watch for students who round to the nearest hundred and leave some people without.

source: A school has 732 people and the principal orders sweets. An item costs 470 rupees and the shopkeeper says around 450 rupees. Which one rounds up and which rounds down? Give one situation for each of: round up, round down, either, exact
video_script.why: The child has met exact and approximate values, and now sees that an approximate number can be more or less than the real one.
video_script.substitution: Rounding up gives an approximate number more than the actual one, rounding down gives one less, and the situation decides which is right.
video_script.anchor: A school of seven hundred thirty two people with a box of sweets, and an item with its price tag.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko rounds seven hundred thirty two to the nearest hundred and orders seven hundred sweets. Seven hundred is less than the number of people, so thirty two people would get none.
video_script.payoff_line: Ordering seven hundred fifty rounds up, and saying around four hundred fifty rounds down

final_answer.value: ordering 750 rounds up; around 450 rounds down
final_answer.spoken: ordering seven hundred fifty rounds up, and saying around four hundred fifty rounds down

never_show: the four situations before step three
maths_rules: the school has 732 people, so at least 732 sweets are needed
ordering 750 sweets: 750 − 732 = 18 more than needed, so the approximate number is more than the actual number: rounding up
the item costs 470 and the shopkeeper says around 450: 470 − 450 = 20 less than the cost, so it is rounding down
500 would be 500 − 470 = 30 more than the cost, so 450 is nearer to 470
round up: food for a group; round down: the time left to catch a bus; either: the distance between two far away places; exact: money in a bank
the slip: 700 sweets for 732 people leaves 732 − 700 = 32 people without
video_script.design: One idea: rounding up gives a number more than the real one, rounding down a number less, and the situation chooses. Wrong idea: Keeko rounds to the nearest hundred and orders too few sweets. The anchor stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part; no hard clear.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, we give a situation for each kind. Rounding up fits buying food for a group, so nobody is left out.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Rounding down fits the time left to catch a bus, so we are not late.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Either way is fine for the distance between two far away places. Exact numbers are needed for money in a bank.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks seven hundred sweets are enough, because seven hundred is the nearest hundred.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But seven hundred is less than seven hundred thirty two. Thirty two people would get no sweet.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>When nobody may be left out, we round up.
